name: Gareth Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential, with no name attached. What does a normal workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the broadband faults row at a contact centre. People call after a router shows every green light but no child in the house can get online, and I check the outage map before sending a line engineer. I have a two-year college diploma, and after seventeen years I am one of the agents colleagues ask when the script stops making sense.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you there, and what is home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like turning a messy fault into one useful instruction, and I use our approved AI search every day for old cases. My wife Sofia works mornings at a laundry, and our grown sons pay their own rent. My lead wage is ordinary for this job, and we have about four months of expenses saved; there are a few other contact centres in reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the faults desk a shortcut is welcome if the outage map still gets checked. The machine can tidy a note, but the engineer should not drive out because an old postcode looked close enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the line faults to keep us busy, and my lead wage to stay. Four months saved covers an ordinary setback, though Sofia's laundry mornings can be shorter in the quiet season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would carry on taking difficult fault calls and show two newer agents how to compare the AI search with the live outage map. In the first year of AI Plateau, I would set aside a small amount from my paid weekend cover if Sofia's normal bills are paid first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough; this is the sort of modest tool I can use. I would be annoyed if the centre treated a faster note as proof that the engineer can be skipped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the search miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family once had no connection because a street cabinet was wet, while the search showed last month's router fault. The live map put six neighbours in the same patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How certain is weekend cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra weekend shift is not guaranteed, so I would save only what it actually pays. Our sons have their own households; they should not be asked to fill ours.

say: I would welcome **faster notes** while checking the live outage map.
I would tell agents **old postcode matches** cannot replace fault evidence.
think: I expect my **lead fault work** and pay to continue.
I value **four months saved**, though laundry hours and weekend cover can vary.
do: Keep taking **difficult fault calls** and show two agents how to check AI search against the live map.
Save a **small weekend amount** only when offered cover pays and usual bills are met.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, with irritation at careless shortcuts.
S0.quote: The machine can tidy a note, but the engineer should not drive out because an old postcode looked close enough.
fieldNote: He already uses **approved AI daily** and teaches map checks in ordinary work.
Extra saving depends on **actual weekend pay** after household bills, not on unoffered overtime or family support.

steps.text: Keep fault calls and show two agents AI-search checks against live outage maps
Save a small amount only from paid weekend cover after usual bills are met

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bot will clear routine router questions, but I want to know who pays for the messy cabinet cases. I would ask the shift manager for the written late rota, not a speech about new opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience may keep me on complex faults, but the centre can combine two rows and cut lead hours. Sofia's laundry pay does not replace my full week, and four months saved would go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would learn the new AI outage matcher by testing twelve closed street-cabinet faults on a paid shift if my manager lets me record errors. In the first year routine chats move, I would keep the paid fault calls offered and compare the written late rota with our bills; if hours fall, I would ask the other centres for their posted paid fault roles before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid hours, though I like checking whether the map tool works. A better diagram does not guarantee a full shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a failed matcher result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark a failure when it names a router while three houses on the same cabinet are down. I would show the supervisor the actual map for each one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave this desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move for the same title on a shorter week. I would accept a posted local role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our bills after the bus fare, keeping this paid desk until a real offer exists.

say: I would ask for the **written late rota** as routine chats move.
I would tell agents **cabinet faults** still need paid investigation.
think: I could lose **lead hours** even if my complex-case skill stays useful.
I cannot replace my **weekly wage** with laundry pay or four months saved.
do: Test **twelve old cabinet faults** with new AI matcher on paid time if error logging is permitted.
Keep **paid fault calls** and compare written hours; if they fall, check posted roles and move only on bill-covering weekly terms.
Keep **current paid calls** until a real written offer exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shifts, though interested in accurate tools.
S1.quote: A better diagram does not guarantee a full shift.
fieldNote: New **AI matcher learning** requires a paid test and permission to log errors.
He would not leave **current paid work** without a real written after-bus-fare offer.

steps.text: Test twelve closed cabinet faults with AI matcher on paid time if error logging allowed
Keep offered paid fault calls and compare written late rota with bills
If hours fall, ask nearby centres about posted paid fault roles
Keep paid calls until real written offer has bill-covering weekly wages and hours after bus fare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sons that thinking AI by 2028 can diagnose or book a line fault before I speak, while hands-on robots arrive around 2031. The field engineer has a later problem; our screens meet it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our paid fault calls to go quickly. Four months of savings give Sofia and me some room to search, but not a wage that lasts until a new employer decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask payroll for written paid-hour plans and put our electricity, rent and food beside the last four payslips. If most of my hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid utility dispatch work; I would accept only written full-week wages and hours covering our bills after travel and keep any paid calls still available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the size of the possible cut, although I can still make a plan. I cannot pay the rent with a nice map of future jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about dispatch work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the dispatch job has paid staff actually speaking to crews or is only an online training place. I would not spend our four months on a course with no posted wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Sofia work more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia could ask her laundry manager about extra mornings, but we would count them only if offered. Our grown sons can talk through an advert with us, not become an income line.

say: I would explain **2028 thinking AI** reaches fault screens before 2031 field robots.
I would ask for **written paid-hour plans** rather than a course poster.
think: I expect **most fault calls** could end quickly.
I cannot treat **four months saved** or unoffered laundry hours as wages.
do: Request **written paid hours** and compare four payslips with household bills.
After most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted dispatch work; accept only written after-travel weekly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a possible major loss of paid calls.
S2.quote: I cannot pay the rent with a nice map of future jobs.
fieldNote: He refuses to count **unoffered laundry hours** or adult-child money as support.
A **posted paid dispatch role** must pass written full-week bill and travel checks.

steps.text: Keep any paid fault calls and request the written paid-hour plan
If most hours end after 2028, apply for posted paid utility dispatch work
Accept only written full-week wages and hours covering bills after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prove whether the new matcher helps with true outages rather than just closing tickets. Thinking AI changes the screens by 2031, and robots reach physical line work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep the hard calls for a while, but I cannot count on the lead rota lasting until I am 63. I would not buy a field-service van on the assumption that robots leave manual work alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for one paid afternoon at the network control desk, if my employer can spare it, to see how outages are sent to crews. I would keep my fault calls and save a little only when weekend cover is actually paid; if my hours fall after 2031, I would check posted control-desk work and its written weekly pay and hours before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own roster, but I can inspect the control desk first. I want to see how the late crew gets sent to a street without an address mix-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you observe in control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the controller phone the crew after a wrong cabinet match, not only watch the screen. That is where the job either solves a fault or sends a van across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot say I will stop at 63. Sofia and I would need verified income and a year of actual bills before reducing either wage.

say: I would ask for a **paid control-desk afternoon** to see actual dispatch work.
I would explain **2031 screen AI** comes before 2034 line-work robots.
think: I cannot rely on my **lead rota** lasting until 63.
I would not buy a **service van** or assume retirement income without evidence.
do: Ask for a **paid control afternoon** if available and keep fault calls.
Save from **actually paid weekend cover**; check posted control work if hours fall after 2031 before applying.
feel: I feel **anxious** about paid hours, with time to inspect another desk.
S3.quote: I would watch the controller phone the crew after a wrong cabinet match, not only watch the screen.
fieldNote: He wants a **paid observation** of crew dispatch, not a speculative course.
Saving depends on **actual weekend cover**, while any role enquiry follows hours falling.

steps.text: Keep paid fault calls and ask for one paid control-desk observation if available
Save a little only from actually paid weekend cover
If hours fall after 2031, inspect posted control jobs' written weekly wages and hours before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sofia a decade lets us mend the household sums while the wage comes in. Thinking AI reaches fault decisions in 2036; hands-on line robots are a later issue around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer late calls, but I cannot name an income that would replace them. Four months saved is a buffer, not a retirement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter Sofia and I would get our actual income statements and list a year of rent, food and electricity. I would keep paid faults work and ask for the lead rota each autumn; after 2036 I would reduce hours only if verified income covers our bills, otherwise keep taking paid calls still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because a decade is long enough to check without pretending the answer is guaranteed. I would rather do the sums than say the boys will look after us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count weekend cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the weekend cover in a separate column because it is not promised every month. A good month of weekend-cover pay cannot be copied into twelve months by writing it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sons have households of their own. We can tell them what we are doing, but I will not add their pay to ours without an actual offer and a real discussion.

say: I would use the **decade** to check household income and bills.
I would say **2036 fault AI** precedes 2039 physical line robots.
think: I cannot name **replacement income** for late calls at 68.
I will not treat **four months saved** or my sons' wages as guaranteed retirement pay.
do: Collect **actual income statements** and a year of bills with Sofia.
Keep **paid fault calls** and ask for lead rota each autumn; reduce hours only if verified income covers bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income, with time to check it.
S4.quote: A good month of weekend-cover pay cannot be copied into twelve months by writing it down.
fieldNote: He separates **variable weekend cover** from regular pay in annual sums.
He keeps **adult-child support** conditional on an actual offer and discussion rather than assuming it will appear.

steps.text: Keep paid fault calls and request the lead rota each autumn
Compare verified income with a year of bills before reducing offered work after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because most fault calls could vanish before another paid dispatch seat opens. Written hours and a real job with full-week money after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the street cabinet when a search result looks tidy. A family needs a working connection, not a polished fault note.

headlineQuote: A family needs a working connection, not a polished fault note.
portrait: A **58-year-old** faults lead with a two-year college diploma and strong call skill.
He uses **AI daily** but verifies its answers on live outage maps.
His **typical lead wage** and four months saved help, while Sofia's laundry shifts can vary.
He checks **actual paid cover** and written full-week job terms before relying on another route.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most paid fault calls before another dispatch seat appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and a real dispatch role with bill-covering pay after travel would help.
